endorsements.quote: We recommend that all implementers building AI chatbots to support behavioral health services consider adopting this or a similar safety monitoring approach that executes rigorous safety guardrails beyond those already available through LLM providers like OpenAI 12.

(1) intentionally building safety guardrails into the chatbot architecture, including templated safety disclaimers (e.g., encouraging 911/988 call for an emergency) output to users upon first use of the chatbot and in response to distress detected in user input;

unlisted_practices: Notify a clinician, care team member, or centralized monitoring service when a chatbot detects high-risk suicide content.
Have trained clinicians or team members monitor chatbot transcripts for suicide risk in near real time, or program the chatbot to alert trained staff when a safety node is activated.
Forward high-risk chatbot content to live human-based emergency resources, or to a clinical team member for chatbots deployed in clinical settings.
Direct chatbot users in crisis to emergency resources through a warm hand-off or direct connection.
Conduct ongoing human expert safety testing of chatbot outputs, especially when new LLM versions are released.
Combine conversational LLMs with rule-based systems, such as neuro-symbolic architectures, to temper unpredictability.
Implement safety planning for all levels of identified suicide risk, including low risk, because risk classification systems have poor predictive accuracy and should not be used in isolation.
Design AI portal-message drafting tools to review messages for suicide and behavioral health risk statements and notify care team members when risk is detected.

screen.reason: Commentary/perspective discussing the risks and preparation needed for AI chatbots responding to patient distress and suicidality.
